title: P-wave and S-wave quiz
description: Watched 'Why does an earthquake shake up and down first, then side to side?' Can you tell a P-wave from an S-wave?

questions.question: An earthquake sends out a P-wave and an S-wave at the same moment. Which one reaches you first?
options: The S-wave, because it shakes harder
questions.explanation: They set off together, but the P-wave is faster (about 6 km per second in the crust, against about 3.5 for the S-wave), so it gets there first.

questions.question: Why does the push-and-pull P-wave travel faster than the sideways S-wave?
options: Because rock is hard to squash and springs straight back, but is easier to push out of shape and slower to recover
Because the P-wave takes a shorter route
questions.explanation: Think of a block of agar-agar: press it from the top and it hardly squashes, springing straight back; push it from the side and it tips easily and takes a while to settle. Rock is the same, only much stiffer.

questions.question: Why does an earthquake often shake up and down first, then side to side?
options: Because earthquakes always happen directly under your house
Because near the surface the waves travel almost straight up: the P-wave pushes along its direction of travel, so up and down, and the S-wave shakes across it, so side to side
Because the P-wave only travels along the surface
questions.explanation: The waves climb from deep underground and arrive almost straight up from below. With travel pointing upwards, P pushes you up and down, while S, at right angles to it, sways you side to side.

questions.question: If the P-wave and S-wave arrive about 35 seconds apart, roughly how far away was the earthquake?
questions.explanation: A simple rule used in Japan: each second of gap is about 8 km. 35 × 8 ≈ 280 km, close to the distance from KL to Penang. It's only a rule of thumb: the factor is about 6 to 8, depending on the region and the depth.

questions.question: How can Japan's earthquake alert go off before the strong shaking?
options: Because the alert predicts the earthquake
Because as soon as seismometers pick up the P-wave, computers do a quick estimate and send the alert electronically, ahead of the S-wave
Because the S-wave carries the alert
questions.explanation: By the time the alert sounds, the earthquake has already happened. Electronic signals are far faster than the S-wave, so the alert can arrive a few seconds to a few tens of seconds early, though very close to the source it may come too late.
